articles_hidden.title: The NF Data Portal: A Community-Driven Resource to Accelerate Neurofibromatosis and Schwannomatosis Research and Drug Development
articles_hidden.authors: Kara Quaid; Belinda B. Garana; Chang In Moon; Aditya Nath; Christina Parry; Efren Munoz; Jineta Banerjee; Alexandra J. Scott; Milen Nikolov; Sang Y. Lee
articles_hidden.abstract:
The NF Data Portal (nf.synapse.org) is a free, open-science platform that centralizes data and resources related to neurofibromatosis (NF) and schwannomatosis (SWN), a group of rare genetic tumor predisposition syndromes. The portal hosts a growing collection of NF and SWN multimodal datasets including genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics and imaging with links to resources such as patient-derived tumor tissue collections, cell lines and preclinical models. The goal of the portal is to provide the broader academic and commercial research community with well-annotated, trusted datasets that can be used in a variety of ways, including asking new scientific questions, benchmarking new methods or tools, and combining datasets across studies. Ultimately, our mission is to accelerate the discovery of treatments and cures for NF and SWN through maximizing the global usability of high-quality data. . 
The NF Data Portal has a cross-institutional backbone of supporters composed of funding organizations, a data coordination center, and a community of clinicians and scientists. Together, this community has developed reusable building blocks for open science, including shared infrastructure, governance frameworks, metadata standards, and a structured data contribution lifecycle. In this publication, we reflect on over a decade of effort to support the data contributor and data user journeys. We share recent platform features and integrations and highlight newly available datasets. 
Whether longtime NF scientists or those encountering this resource for the first time, the NF Data Portal provides access to one of the largest NF datasets available to advance academic research, industry-driven discovery and therapeutic development. For industry users, the portal serves as a strategic translational research asset that supports target validation, biomarker discovery, patient stratification and data-driven decision making, helping to de-risk development programs and inform clinical strategy. As AI-driven analytical methods transform biomedical research, richly annotated, disease-specific datasets like those housed in the NF Data Portal, will be essential raw material for developing and validating new tools and novel treatments.

articles.title: Record Linkage Error and Inference in Population Research
articles.abstract: The explosion in digitization of large-scale administrative data and advances in record linkage have opened up new possibilities for studying core topics in population research, including social mobility, early-life determinants of longevity, and shifts in ethnoracial identity. Much attention has been paid to improving record linkage algorithms, but methodological guidance for researchers analyzing linked data is limited. We propose a general framework to explain how different types of linkage errors—false matches and missed matches—impact inference with linked data and introduce a bias-correction method. We then conduct three empirical case studies on canonical topics in population research: social mobility, the education–longevity gradient, and shifts in ethnoracial identification. These case studies demonstrate the settings in which linkage errors do and do not meaningfully impact substantive research findings. We conclude with practical recommendations for researchers performing inference with linked data and provide an accompanying R package implementing the methods introduced in this paper.

articles.title: Cognitive Degradation: The Reconfiguration of the Labor Process and Knowledge Authority in the Era of Generative Artificial Intelligence
articles.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is increasingly entering knowledge-intensive work, including programming, writing, design, analysis, and management. Unlike earlier forms of automation that were often concentrated on physical operations or clearly defined executional tasks, generative AI can produce text, code, classifications, and proposals within the workflow itself. Its significance therefore lies not simply in the displacement of particular tasks, but in the possibility that activities once associated with professional judgment become increasingly mediated by corporate technological systems. This paper examines that possibility through the concept of “cognitive degradation.” Drawing on Marx’s analysis of machinery and fixed capital, Braverman’s account of labor-process control and deskilling (Braverman, 1974), and Burawoy’s emphasis on worker agency and consent (Burawoy, 1978; 1979), the paper defines cognitive degradation narrowly. It occurs when AI takes over cognitive tasks previously performed by workers, workers’ effective authority over the criteria and application of judgment declines, and that shift is stabilized through organizational rules, technological systems, or labor institutions. The concept therefore should not be treated as synonymous with deskilling, declining productivity, or algorithmic management. To explore the mechanism, the paper examines three ideal types rather than three directly comparable causal cases: boundary-setting in the Writers Guild of America (WGA), internalization in AI-assisted software development, and institutional mediation through German co-determination. The cases show that AI can increase productivity without necessarily reducing workers’ skills, while still altering how knowledge and judgment are organized. The paper argues that the central issue in AI-mediated labor is therefore not whether machines replace workers, but whether workers retain meaningful authority over the definition, evaluation, and application of knowledge. The paper further proposes that sustained changes in such authority may affect occupational autonomy, skill formation, and bargaining power. Claims about macro-level class restructuring, however, remain propositions for future empirical research rather than conclusions established by the cases examined here.

articles.title: 한국의 복지균열 부상에 관한 연구
articles.abstract:
이 연구의 목적은 경제성장담론이 지배적이던 한국정치에서 복지담론 및 전선이 부상한
요인을 규명하는 것이다. 경제 구조의 변화의 기존 규범에의 작용 및 시민사회 내 헤게모니를
둘러싼 담론투쟁 이론을 통해 2009년 무상급식부터 2012년 대선 시기 복지담론의 활성화 및
복지균열의 부상 요인을 추적하였다.
저 발달한 발전주의 복지레짐과 신자유주의 경제정책의 연계된 정책효과는 사회양극화, 빈
곤층 확대 등을 초래하였고, 이것은 ‘경제성장이 민생문제를 해결한다’는 기존의 규범을 약화
시켰다. 경제성장이 민생문제를 해결한다고 주장하고 집권한 이명박 정부의 정당성이 약화되
고, 2009년 경기교육감과 경기의회의 갈등을 계기로 무상급식 논쟁이 촉발하였다. 그리고 시
민사회 내 시민, 사회단체들은 사적이익을 공적이익으로 전환하고, 사회적 정당성을 획득하기
위한 담론투쟁을 전개한다. 이를 통해 국민여론이 무상급식 및 복지에 대한 지지로 변화하였
다. 복지에 대한 국민적 지지를 확인한 정당들은 특정 위기 국면에서 복지를 수용할 정치적
이익이 있는 세력 우선적으로 복지를 수용하게 된다. 그리고 여론, 시민사회단체들의 계속적인
압력 속에서, 선거에서 복지 이슈를 선점하기 위해 양당은 전면적으로 복지를 수용하고, 이후
이것은 경제민주화담론으로 이어지게 된다.

articles.title: A study on the influence of social movements on political representation focusing on the minimum wage case in the mid- 2010s American states
articles.abstract: This study examines how the social movement can contribute to improving political representation with the case of the minimum wage legislation in American states after 2012. The contribution of this research is that it’s an empirical analysis of how social movement affects the legislative process, especially in the agenda-setting stage and how social discourse takes part in this process, given the lack of research concerning determinants of the state legislation of the higher minimum wage, especially focusing on the influence of the social movement on the legislation. I analyze the impact of the social movement, measured by the media exposure frequency, on public opinion, the proposal of bills and the legislation with the national-level time serial and the state-level data. I investigate the impact of the social discourse on public opinion and the legislative process to illuminate the underlying mechanism where the social movement affects the political outcome. The social movement contributes to the improvement of political representation by spreading the social discourse, setting the agenda in civic and political society and triggering partisan politics for institutional change.

articles.title: Value-Based Adaptive Reuse: Design and Initial Testing of a Serious-Game Prototype
articles.abstract: Adaptive reuse of heritage buildings requires stakeholders, and more specifically, architects to navigate interdependent questions of heritage significance, contemporary function, environmental performance, community benefit, financial feasibility, and approval of other stakeholders (developers, investors, and regulators). Process models can structure these questions, yet conventional validation methods reveal only part of how practitioners move between them under constraint. This paper presents the design and pilot testing of Architect's Design Challenge, a tabletop serious-game prototype developed to explore professional decision-making in adaptive reuse and to examine the practical legibility of the Effective Adaptive Reuse of Heritage Buildings (EARHB) process model. Players progress through six stations, allocate limited resources, select action cards, respond to stakeholder requirements, and construct a design proposition using four predefined project-value categories represented by coloured components. Two formative test rounds, involving students and architects, were organised around introduction, gameplay, and debriefing. The tests indicated that the prototype could stimulate explicit discussion of priorities, sequencing, resource allocation, and trade-offs. They also revealed a central design tension: abstraction supported strategic play but sometimes weakened correspondence with professional practice, particularly for expert players. The study contributes a transparent mapping between research constructs and game mechanics, identifies requirements for future validation, and shows how serious gaming could make selected moments of value recognition, translation into design choices, negotiation, and revision observable within a simulated decision pathway. The evidence is exploratory. It does not establish learning effects, behavioural validity, or transfer to real projects.

articles.title: Insufficiently Affordable: Public Opinion About Housing Affordability
articles.authors: Tali Mendelberg; Gustavo Novoa; Adrian C. Pietrzak
articles.abstract: Americans want government to improve housing affordability. Yet proposals for affordable housing often encounter public resistance. We argue for a neglected explanation: concerns that these proposals are insufficiently affordable. Using four original surveys with novel, precise measures of affordability and randomized developer and landlord profiteering, we find wide support for affordable housing when it primarily benefits people of low means and does not favor developer or landlord profiteering. This support holds even when the hypothetical building is proposed in the respondent’s neighborhood, support entails tradeoffs and costly behavior in the survey, and the policy requires tax increases. The tax finding replicates in election outcomes of actual ballot measures. Pro-poor sentiments shape these preferences, above and beyond self-interest, and offset the negative impact of racial attitudes. Buildings and policies that satisfy these sentiments draw much higher public support. However, common policies fail to do so.

articles.title: Knowledge to action in alternative crisis response: Examining alignment and misalignment between evidence and practice
articles.authors: Megan Wheeler Rowe; Claire Ryder; Amanda Mathew; Jenny Angela Hui; Brandon Barksdale; Leyna Lowe; Andrew David Eaton
articles.abstract:
Background: Alternative crisis response models have rapidly emerged to reorganize mental health crisis care away from traditional police-led responses. It is important to explore whether the existing evidence base on co-response and civilian-led models aligns with the perspectives of those closest to the field.
Aims: This study examined points of alignment and misalignment between synthesized evidence from two scoping reviews and the lived, practice-based, and systems-level knowledge of key informants in alternative crisis response.
Methods: From August-December 2025, 33 crisis response key informants in Canada and the United States participated in semi-structured interviews prompted by the scoping reviews. Data were analyzed using directed qualitative content analysis, with 13 sensitizing domains regarding key processes of co-response and civilian-led models.
Results. Participants strongly aligned with reducing police involvement and developing distinct crisis response teams. Misalignment most often appeared as contextualization or extension, especially around police involvement, interprofessional collaboration, team composition, local service capacity, and public narratives. Domains related to monitoring, evaluation, and model variation had high counts of no available data.
Conclusions: Findings suggest that evidence on alternative crisis response is broadly resonant but requires contextualization to reflect the realities of practice and the sustainability needs of a rapidly evolving field.

articles.title: Are we nursing the technologies? An ethnographic study of nurses’ tech work and its implications for well-being
articles.authors: Paulien D'Huyvetter; Ellen Algera; Daantje Derks; Pascale Marie Le Blanc; Iris Wallenburg; Rik Wehrens
articles.abstract: Healthcare systems across the world face persistent nursing shortages. Although technological innovations are widely promoted as solutions to rising workloads and staff shortages, they also generate additional, largely invisible forms of work. We examine nurses’ tech work: the unanticipated work nurses perform to keep hospital technologies functioning. Drawing on insights from Science and Technology Studies and Work and Organizational Psychology, we investigate the types of tech work nurses perform and their implications for nurses’ well-being. Based on ethnographically grounded observations, interviews, and focus groups conducted in a Dutch academic hospital, we identify eight types of tech work in nursing. For each type, we show tech work can negatively affect nurses’ well-being through hindrance demands and reduced perceptions of meaningfulness, particularly when combined with other demanding tasks. Our findings suggest that the challenge is not the deployment of more technologies, but their design and implementation in ways that minimize burdensome tech work and better support nurses’ care practices.

articles.title: Does Democratic and Economic Benchmarking Matter for Affective Polarization? A Survey Experiment in Poland
articles.abstract: This article examines whether international benchmarking, cross-national comparisons of a country’s democratic or economic performance, intensifies affective polarization among citizens. While prior research has shown that international economic comparisons shape electoral behavior, little is known about how such external evaluations influence emotional hostility between partisan groups. Drawing on a survey experiment conducted as part of the 2023 Polish National Election Study, the study tests whether exposure to negative international assessments increases affective polarization. The results reveal a striking asymmetry. Exposure to democratic benchmarking, information signaling Poland’s decline on democratic indicators relative to regional peers, significantly increases affective polarization, whereas economic benchmarking produces no comparable effect. These effects are conditional. Democratic benchmarking polarizes primarily among citizens with negative evaluations of the outgoing government, while leaving strong government supporters unaffected. The findings suggest that benchmarking is most polarizing when it concerns identity-relevant and normatively charged domains in which responsibility can be credibly attributed to domestic political actors. Overall, the study shows that international reputational cues can deepen partisan divides, reinforcing emotional boundaries between political camps rather than fostering a common ground for evaluating national performance.

articles.title: Transforming Public Sector Corporations in Tanzania: A Capability-Based Framework for Addressing Persistent Governance, Financial, and Organizational Weaknesses
articles.abstract: Public and Statutory Corporations (PSCs) remain important instruments for economic transformation, strategic investment, and public service delivery in developing economies. Governments establish PSCs to address market failures, provide essential services, support industrial development, and advance national economic objectives. However, despite growing interest in PSCs' governance, several gaps remain in existing literature. First, many studies focus primarily on ownership structures, privatization outcomes, and financial performance while paying limited attention to internal institutional capabilities. Second, existing performance assessments frequently identify weaknesses without developing systematic approaches for measuring recurring organizational constraints. Third, limited attention has been given to mechanisms that translate oversight findings into continuous organizational improvement. The study, therefore, addresses these gaps by developing the Public Sector Corporation Performance Weakness Index (PSC-PWI), an analytical framework designed to identify and measure recurring institutional weaknesses affecting PSCs' performance.

articles.title: Exclusion by inclusion: How diverse sex/gender measures can inadvertently contribute to the exclusion of beyond-binary respondents from survey-based research
articles.authors: Leonie C Steckermeier; Alba María Kugelmeier López; Stephanie Hess
articles.abstract:
This paper illustrates how the inclusion of beyond-binary gender measures in large-scale population surveys can inadvertently contribute to the exclusion of the very populations they aim to represent. Recent international and EU efforts to integrate more inclusive sex and gender measures in surveys aim to improve data collection for evidence-based policymaking. While best practices in operationalization, reporting, and data protection have received substantial attention, the potential challenges of making sex/gender minorities identifiable in survey data remain largely overlooked. 
Based on examples from three established surveys in political and social science research—the European Social Survey, the International Social Survey Programme, and the Eurobarometer—we illustrate how more inclusive gender measures can render beyond-binary respondents vulnerable to exclusion, due to questionnaire design, data protection practices, and methodological challenges arising from their small numbers. We conclude with recommendations for questionnaire design and routing, data collection and documentation, and the analytical treatment of beyond-binary respondents.

articles.title: How Organizations Involved in Criminal Activity Sway Public Opinion: An Integrative Framework of Discursive Legitimation Strategies From a Scoping Review
articles.authors: Kristina Sabrina Weißmüller; Tijs van den Broek; Jana S. Krawinkel; Steven James Watson
articles.abstract: This study examines how organizations involved in criminal activities try to publicly legitimize their actions by using discursive legitimation strategies. Often involving moral neutralization and blame deflection techniques, these discursive strategies present organizations involved in criminal activities as virtuous and justified to evade punishment and undermine public support for law enforcement. Although discursive legitimation strategies result in societal harm, little is known about what types of strategies exist for criminal activities, how they differ, and whether they change legitimacy judgments. Based on a framework that integrates the communicative aspects of legitimation and strategic ambiguity, this scoping review identifies, categorizes, and synthesizes the empirical evidence on discursive legitimation strategies used by organizations involved in criminal activities. We identify 10 strategies that are conceptually linked with different legitimacy dimensions and develop testable propositions about how five distinct mechanisms—licensing, contestation, enculturation, neutralization, and cleansing—are used to create strategic ambiguity. This study elevates our understanding of discursive legitimation strategies used to justify illegitimate and criminal practices to sway public opinion and informs practice on how to develop countermeasures and strengthen societal resilience against criminal manipulation.

articles.title: Sociotechnical Transition and Uncertainty in the Lithium Mining Industry: Technologies, Politics and Transparency
articles.authors: Iván Ojeda-Pereira; Sebastián Herrera-León; Marcelo Lufin; Fernando Campos-Medina
articles.abstract: Technological transitions in extractive industries are commonly assessed through technical and environmental performance, whilst their social and ethical dimensions receive little systematic attention. This article addresses that gap through the adoption of direct lithium extraction (DLE) technologies in Chile, the world’s second largest lithium producer and the leading producer from salt flats. The National Lithium Strategy promotes these technologies as a response to social tensions over the use of water and brine in fragile ecosystems, and the conditions of their implementation remain open. Drawing on interdisciplinary work between the engineering sciences and the social sciences, we ask which technological and social uncertainties experts identify in this transition. Two expert workshops were held with 20 participants from industry, the State and academia, and their contributions were examined through inductive qualitative content analysis. The findings show five uncertainties: (i) there is no consensus on which technologies will be implemented or on the criteria for choosing them; (ii) the effects of brine reinjection lack conclusive evidence; (iii) the role and agency of the State remain undetermined; (iv) no mapping exists of the actors regarded as valid participants in the debate; and (v) there is no agreement on how the social sustainability of this change should be measured. We propose five public information infrastructures as a design response to these uncertainties, whilst acknowledging that transparency is a necessary but not sufficient condition for ethical sociotechnical governance in the extractive industries of the Global South.

articles.title: The Q18 Survey: Initial Validation of an Employee-Reported Outcomes
articles.abstract: Employee surveys commonly assess individual attitudes and experiences, but fewer instruments integrate these with employees’ perceptions of organisational functioning. This study reports the initial validation of the Q18, a brief employee-reported outcomes instrument designed for employee listening, aggregate-level human resource and managerial monitoring, and perceived organisational assessment. A validation study was conducted with 3,350 employees working in France. Analyses examined score distributions, reliability, confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) structure, discriminant validity, multi-group invariance, multicollinearity, and practical and nomological anchoring with the employee Net Promoter Score (eNPS). CFA model comparisons supported a correlated eight-factor structure comprising four individual outcomes and four perceived organisational outcomes. Reliability estimates were compatible with aggregate-level interpretation for human resource and managerial tracking, and invariance analyses supported measurement stability across the main segmentation variables. Q18 scores increased progressively across eNPS detractors, passives, and promoters. Discriminant validity received partial support: the dimensions were empirically distinguishable, but some remained strongly interdependent.  By bringing together individual outcomes and perceived organisational outcomes, the Q18 provides an integrated interpretation of tensions or alignments between employee experience and perceived collective functioning and helps extend employee listening practices beyond the measurement of individual attitudes alone. Further research is needed to establish its longitudinal, organisational-level, and cross-cultural validity.

articles.title: Using Geospatial modeling to Understand Spatial Job Access for TANF Recipients
articles.authors: Gabriel Appiah; Arthi Rao; Latrice Rollins; Andrew Cooper; Alex Camardelle
articles.abstract: Access to employment is central to the effectiveness of the Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF) program, yet job opportunities are unevenly distributed across space. This study examines county-level patterns in job accessibility for TANF recipients, with a particular focus on African American (AA) populations and urban–rural differences in commuting behavior. Using data from Alabama, Louisiana, Georgia, Virginia, and the District of Columbia, we construct gravity-based job accessibility indices for high-, median-, and low-paying employment. Distance-decay parameters are empirically estimated from Longitudinal Employer–Household Dynamics (LEHD) commuting flows, allowing travel sensitivity to vary between urban and rural areas. Accessibility measures are computed for total employment and compared across AA TANF - majority and minority counties. We then apply hierarchical clustering to county-level indicators of accessibility, socioeconomic vulnerability, housing and mobility constraints, and TANF caseload composition. The resulting seven-cluster typology reveals distinct TANF opportunity contexts, including counties characterized by severe spatial isolation and others where high accessibility coexists with persistent disadvantage. These findings highlight the limitations of uniform TANF work requirements and support the need for place-sensitive, equity-oriented welfare policy design.

articles.title: Strategic behaviour in decision support systems: a conceptual framework for observation in multi-stakeholder decision-making processes
articles.authors: Monique Arkesteijn; Adinda Jongkind; Fatemeh Hedieh Arfa; Haiko van der Voort
articles.abstract:
While DSS are designed to enhance transparency and provide structure in complex, multi-stakeholder settings, they also influence actions of participating stakeholders and thereby their strategic choices. This paper reviews the literature on SB and DSS, identifies diverse forms of strategic action, and proposes a five-step framework for systematically observing SB in DSS-supported processes and environments.
The framework integrates contextual dynamics, stakeholder motivations, strategic approaches, and resource use, offering a structured and comprehensive lens for analysis. By focusing on how stakeholders engage strategically in practice, rather than prescribing how they should behave, the framework enables a nuanced and realistic understanding of stakeholder interaction, behaviour, and power in participatory settings. This conceptual contribution advances both academic and applied discussions by providing a tool that supports empirical investigation as well as the design and use of DSS in real-world decision-making contexts.

articles.title: the em—dash fails to em–erge: a registered null result for U+2014 in Polish and an exploratory function-word shift in 60,275 Sejm interpellations, 2015–2025
articles.abstract:
Since the release of ChatGPT (30 November 2022) a belief has spread that the em-dash "—" reveals text written with the help of a language model. This preregistered study tested that claim on 60,275 single-author written parliamentary questions (interpelacje) submitted to the Polish Sejm between 2015 and 2025. The decision rule was registered on OSF before the data were seen.

The cue does not work in Polish. The registered hypothesis was not confirmed: in the decisive cell the share of documents containing an em-dash rose by 1.73 percentage points, but the confidence interval of that difference includes zero (−4.44 to +8.07 pp), so the second condition of the two-part decision rule was not satisfied, and three registered disconfirmation conditions fired. Follow-up tests point to the cause: models writing in Polish, and machine-translation flows, put a shorter dash there – the en-dash "–". The marker is anglocentric and is not suitable for Polish.

An exploratory analysis measured something else: the frequency of Polish closed-class words (conjunctions, prepositions, particles) that a writer does not choose consciously. The reference point was an independently published corpus of Polish human-written and model-written texts, frozen together with its reading rule before measurement. From 2024 the distribution of these words moves toward the profile of the models (rank correlation rho = +0.368; 95% CI +0.228 to +0.461), while at a placebo date – the 2019 change of parliamentary term, where no such effect is expected – it does not move at all (−0.070; difference +0.438, +0.221 to +0.611). The shift survives four term-change controls.

The change is small but widespread, and that is the correct description of its strength. Inside a single parliamentary office it is barely visible (median rho +0.125), yet it points the same way in 61 of 84 offices that could be measured separately (72.6%, one-sided p = 2·10⁻⁵), against 53.8% at the control date, which is what chance produces.

There is no sudden jump at the date of the ChatGPT release. The change becomes visible in 2024 and unambiguous in 2025, and the shape of the transition (ramp versus late step) is not identified. The result describes a shift across a whole population of documents and allows no statement about the authorship of any single document or about any individual member of parliament. It does not establish a cause: changes in office staff, in subject matter and in editing practice remain possible explanations alongside tools. An independent reimplementation, with no access to the author's code, reproduced the corpus, the deduplication, the author panel and the headline analyses from raw HTML down.

articles.title: CLAIM: Calibration of Legitimacy through AI Messaging - A Theory of How Conversational AI Shapes Minority and Majority Voices in Group Deliberation
articles.authors: Hoang Phuong Nhi Do; Suzanne van Gils; Christoph Lutz
articles.abstract: Conversational artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly shapes communicative spaces preceding social interaction, yet its effects are often studied in isolation from subsequent group dynamics. Recognizing this gap, we propose the Calibration of Legitimacy through AI Messaging (CLAIM) theory, which argues that pre-deliberative AI interaction calibrates perceived opinion legitimacy and shapes voice in group deliberation. Drawing on AI sycophancy, the Spiral of Silence, and multi-level legitimacy literature, CLAIM proposes that high AI sycophancy increases validity and propriety beliefs, whereas opposition from AI deflates them. Moreover, structural opinion status moderates these effects: AI sycophancy can generate a compensatory voice effect for opinion-minority participants, while AI challenge can produce compounded silencing. Additionally, a legitimacy shock may emerge when minority-opinion holders encounter group compositions that contradict AI-calibrated legitimacy beliefs. Together, CLAIM extends AI sycophancy research by theorizing conversational AI as a legitimacy-calibrating force that can reshape voice in group deliberation, particularly under structural communicative inequality.

articles.title: Detecting Coordinated Posting Behavior on Social Media. Introducing and Evaluating the Embedding-Based Tool ‘coorsim’
articles.abstract: The detection of coordinated behavior on social media is an effective heuristic for uncovering organized manipulation of online publics. Existing detection tools rely on identifying identical or lexically similar content disseminated rapidly by networks of accounts. However, these tools are ill-suited to detect the coordinated posting of semantically similar content. This is a shortcoming in the age of LLMs that enable the large-scale generation of diverse yet semantically equivalent content. In this paper, we introduce and systematically evaluate coorsim, an open source R package for for detecting semantically similar coordinated posting. The package provides a platform-agnostic end-to-end workflow encompassing embedding retrieval, coordinated community detection, automated community labeling, and visualization. We systematically evaluate its performance against the most comprehensive benchmark dataset of known influence operations to date, covering 15 international campaigns. Across 3,780 evaluated parameter combinations, the best stable configuration achieved an overall F1 of 0.69. Using multilevel Bayesian regression models, we isolated the influence of parameter choices. We also provide a qualitative assessment of automatically generated community labels. Our results demonstrate that coorsim provides a valid, albeit not flawless, contribution to closing a gap in the landscape of computational tools for detecting coordinated online behavior.

articles.title: What Drives Legislative Anger? Multimodal Evidence from South Korea's National Assembly
articles.abstract: Legislative anger is often understood as expressive representation, a signal that legislators passionately defend constituent interests. We argue that partisan blame underpins these displays, especially when parties attack one another over alleged misconduct. Using deep-learning models, we measure vocal and facial anger across 355 hours of plenary debate in South Korea's 20th National Assembly (2016-2020), covering 11,060 speech segments by 247 legislators. We find that anger peaks when legislators discuss scandal, at twice the level of policy debate. Moreover, a quasi-experiment around the impeachment of President Park Geun-hye shows that the same legislators become angrier in opposition and calmer in government. These findings challenge accounts that treat legislative anger primarily as constituency signaling and highlight how partisan blame and institutional position shape emotional expression in legislatures.

articles.title: LINGUISTIC STRATEGIES IN MISINFORMATION: A SEMANTIC-PRAGMATIC FRAMEWORK FOR DETECTING MANIPULATION IN MEDIA DISCOURSE
articles.abstract: This article identifies recurrent patterns of linguistic behaviour characteristic of misinformation and proposes a semantic-pragmatic approach to analysing manipulation in media texts. Through the application of five mechanisms – implicature (GRICE, 1975; HORN, 2011; SPERBER; WILSON, 1995), presupposition (SCHLENKER, 2011; SIMONS, 2005; STALNAKER, 1973), modality (VON FINTEL, 2006), genericity (CARLSON, 2011; MÜLLER, 2003), and deverbal nominalisation (GRIMSHAW, 1990, 2011) – it demonstrates how these resources are exploited to constrain inferential paths and generate interpretive distortions. Although other mechanisms are available, the study focuses on these five because they are most frequently exploited in misinformation discourse. The analysis identifies five main manipulative strategies: (1) the suggestion of misleading meanings through implicatures, which allow the speaker to maintain plausible deniability by keeping manipulative content outside the truth-conditional level of the utterance; (2) the naturalisation of controversial content as established fact; (3) the exploitation of modal asymmetry to obscure the boundary between speculative possibility and normative necessity; (4) the promotion of essentialist universalisations through generic and vague reference; and (5) the suppression of information about agents and responsibilities. These strategies are exemplified by a 2023 news story on inclusive terminology in healthcare, which serves as a paradigmatic case for revealing the linguistic architecture of misinformation. The results contribute to the semantics-pragmatics interface by operationalising the distinction between what is said and what is implicated, and by revealing the recurrent patterns through which ordinary pragmatic mechanisms are strategically exploited to produce manipulative effects in media discourse.

articles.title: From Division to Action? Mobilizing Women Through Gender Inequality Framing
articles.abstract: Though American women face significant economic, political, and social inequality, it has been far more challenging to mobilize women around this inequality than some other groups. In this paper, I use a multi-method approach to causally examine how women respond to mobilization efforts from women's movements and organizations. First, in a survey experiment, I find that frames that raise awareness of gender inequality and emphasize the need to build on women's progress significantly influence women's participatory intentions and political attitudes. To examine effects among those who are already engaged around issues of inequality, I then conduct a field experiment with a women's political organization. Results from this study suggest more mixed effects of outreach about gender inequality and progress, with null effects on email engagement yet increases in donation behavior. This paper has important implications for academic research on political behavior and applied strategies to engage women in the context of recent social movements and elections.

articles.title: No drain, no gain? The problems with unequal exchange
articles.abstract: Recent empirical work (Hickel et al. 2021, 2022) appears to show that the Global South is being ``drained" of resources and value on a vast scale through unequal exchange (UE) and/or ecologically unequal exchange (EUE). Headline estimates of the aggregate value of this extraction have been widely taken to substantiate two politico-normative issues: that the South is systematically exploited through international price formation, and that this drain constitutes a binding constraint on Southern development and a precondition for Northern prosperity. This paper argues that neither claim is supported by the new measurement agenda. It shows that new drain estimates rely on untenable premises -- in particular, claims of North-South parity in productivity and export composition. Stipped of these assumptions, Hickel et al's method can't yield a counterfactual ``fair price" vector, meaning that their estimates are ungrounded and indeterminate. Moreover, even granting the estimates, they do not sustain an underdevelopment thesis. In standard growth regressions and long-run club-convergence tests, higher measured drain is non-negative and often positively associated with Southern growth once conventional fundamentals are controlled for. The paper suggests ways that research in ecological economics can be placed on a firmer conceptual footing.

articles.title: Branding at the Water’s Edge: Perceived Elite Polarization of Ukraine Aid, 2022–2024
articles.authors: Haoran Shi; Wanting Wang; Dario Krpan
articles.abstract: United States assistance to Ukraine began with broad bipartisan support and acquired a durable partisan structure within eighteen months. We treat that transformation as a naturally occurring case for observing party brand formation, which requires parties both to occupy distinct positions and to speak about those positions consistently. Drawing on 37,312 sentences from 11,819 news articles published between March 2022 and December 2024, we annotated each sentence on one general aid dimension and three explanatory dimensions using a large language model, masking party and politician references so that positions were recovered from what a sentence conveys rather than from prior association with a party. Aggregating to articles and then to months produced continuous series of between-party polarization and within-party message coherence as represented in news coverage, which we combined into a Party Brand Index. Polarization on General Ukraine Aid Stance increased, with the fitted gap between the final and initial months widening by 11.71 points, and it did so through three persistent level shifts rather than gradual drift. Both parties moved toward opposition and Republicans moved further. Among the explanatory dimensions, the framing that set foreign commitments against domestic priorities aligned most closely with the aid stance gap, although that ordering did not survive dependence-preserving resampling. Neither party's message coherence tracked polarization from month to month, yet Republican coverage converged substantially across the period while Democratic coverage did not. Brand formation was therefore neither smooth, nor symmetric, nor synchronized, and the two conditions a brand requires advanced within the same party on different schedules.

articles.title: How Segregation Fuels the Far Right: Higher-Educated Social Relationships Buffer the Politically Radicalizing Effect of Economic Insecurity
articles.abstract:
In recent decades, economic insecurity has driven some lower-educated voters
to the far right, while others have not moved. We argue that segregation explains
this variation: Higher-educated friends and relatives hold relatively progressive
views and norms against the far right, preventing lower-educated citizens from
politically translating economic insecurity into far-right support. Using existing
panel data from the Netherlands and original data from the U.S. and Germany,
we find that lower-educated individuals in higher-educated networks are much less
likely to respond to economic insecurity by moving to the far right. Differential
access to economic resources does not explain this effect. Rather, novel network
modules and an experimental manipulation of network salience show that network
education levels condition how individuals politicize insecurity. These findings show
that others affect how we make political sense of change, and suggest that societal
resilience against growing far-right appeal depends on the mutual integration of its
citizens.

articles.title: Statistischer Quartalsbericht 3/2022
articles.authors: Amt für Statistik und Wahlen Stadt Leipzig
articles.abstract: Regelmäßige vierteljährliche Veröffentlichung: Textbeiträge zu ausgewählten Themen (Teil 1) und statistische Daten (Teil 2)

articles.title: Classification testing: A new framework for drawing qualitative conclusions from quantitative estimates
articles.abstract: Social scientists rely on hypothesis testing to support their research conclusions, but the standard tests are designed for testing one hypothesis rather than adjudicating between rival possibilities.  We develop a new framework, "classification testing", as an alternative. Instead of selecting one hypothesis to test, a researcher conducting a classification test decides what qualitative distinctions ("classes") are most substantively relevant; the test either assigns the estimand to a class  with error control similar to that of a conventional hypothesis test,  or declares the result inconclusive. We argue that classification testing is superior to current practice not just when the objective is to adjudicate between rival possibilities but also when there is one research hypothesis to be tested, because classification testing exposes that hypothesis to refutation.  We illustrate the framework by applying it to a well-known media experiment and offer an R package to aid in implementation.

articles.title: Authoritarian Lenses and the Dynamics of Exclusion: The Radical Right in Chile
articles.authors: Lisa Zanotti; Fabian Villalobos-Machuca; Francisco Roldán Duque; Joaquín Valenzuela-Pastén; Sofía Cuadra
articles.abstract: This chapter examines the Chilean radical right through conceptual lenses developed primarily in the European context, using the case to assess the limits of those categories beyond their region of origin. It advances two conceptual claims. First, drawing on Stenner (2005), it argues that authoritarianism is better understood not as an ideology on a par with nativism, but as an individual predisposition activated by perceived normative threat — a lens through which social change is interpreted rather than a fixed doctrine. Second, it argues that nativism, understood as the fusion of nationalism and xenophobia in defence of ethnic homogeneity, is too narrow for a region where migration flows involve culturally proximate populations, and that civic-cultural nationalism captures the Chilean case more accurately. The chapter traces the rise of José Antonio Kast and the Republican Party and the subsequent emergence of the Libertarian Party and Team Patriota, and shows how authoritarian predispositions combine with nationalist, anti-feminist and anti-communist frames to construct migrants, feminists, sexual minorities and leftist actors as outgroups.

articles.title: How Do Voters Respond to Gradual Climate Costs?  Evidence from the Insurance Crisis
articles.abstract: Climate change is transforming the U.S. economy in gradual but increasingly impactful ways. Existing literature on climate shocks and economic transformation is poorly positioned to explain how these gradual costs shape opinions and behavior. I study this through the U.S. home insurance market. Using panel data (2016–2024) and 246 million insurance records, I show voters recognize the insurance crisis and shift away from homeownership in response, but that rate increases do not significantly change climate opinions. With original survey data, I explain why: voters fail to attribute insurance costs to climate change and to connect insurance to climate policy. I trace this gap to the information environment: analysis of posts from 3,000 public officials and 2.9 million news articles shows that neither officials nor media frequently link insurance to climate change. These findings advance understanding of how gradual climate costs are—and are not—reshaping American opinion and behavior.

articles.title: Co-Writing the Self: Conversational AI as a Reflective Partner in Narrative Identity Reconstruction
articles.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in writing and reflective practice, yet limited empirical research has examined how sustained interaction with conversational AI may mediate narrative identity. This study explores how ongoing engagement with ChatGPT shaped self-reflection, authorship, authenticity, and the interpretation of lived experience. Guided by an interpretivist paradigm, the study employed analytic autoethnography based on sustained interaction with ChatGPT across a purposively bounded longitudinal conversational corpus on academic, professional, and personal contexts. Conversational transcripts and reflective journal records were analysed using Reflexive Thematic Narrative Analysis, integrating Narrative Identity Theory and Post-Phenomenology. Analysis identified interconnected processes through which ChatGPT shifted from an information tool towards a reflective conversational partner, supported narrative integration, mediated reflection and decision-making, and prompted ongoing negotiation of authenticity and human authorship. ChatGPT contributed linguistic formulation, conceptual organisation, and alternative interpretive possibilities; however, experiential ownership, evaluative authority, and ethical responsibility remained with the researcher. The study develops the Human–AI Narrative Co-Construction Framework (HANCF) to conceptualise narrative reconstruction as a recursive process of AI-mediated reflection governed by human evaluative and narrative authority. The findings suggest that conversational AI may participate in narrative identity reconstruction without possessing narrative identity or displacing human authorship. The study contributes an autoethnographic account of sustained human–AI interaction and offers a framework for understanding how reflective partnership with conversational AI may extend human meaning-making while preserving experiential and ethical authority.

articles.title: Social Stressors and Gender Inequalities in Post-COVID-19 Syndrome: Evidence from a Population-Based Cohort in Germany
articles.authors: Nicolai Gröpler; Meike Dirks; Andrea Hildebrandt; Thomas Keil; Ann-Kathrin Knak; Sina M. Pütz; Mandy Roheger; Antje Wulff; Gundula Zoch
articles.abstract: Women report post-COVID-19 symptoms more often and more severely than men, but the contribu-tion of socially structured stress exposure to this difference is largely unexamined. Social stressors are particularly relevant in the context of infectious diseases such as COVID-19, as they may influ-ence health outcomes through hormonal processes and their impact on immune function. This study examines whether stressors and coping resources in work and family life are associated with post-COVID-19 symptoms and whether they account for sex/gender differences in it. Integrating psycho-logical and sociological perspectives with contemporary medical knowledge, we hypothesized that social stressors influence the development of post-COVID-19 symptoms and, in part, explain sex and other socio-economic disparities. We utilized data from population-based COVIDOM study within the German National Pandemic Cohort Network (NAPKON-POP, 2020-23, N=2,941), recruited by local health authorities on the basis of a positive PCR test irrespective of symptom burden. 86 per-cent of women vs 76 of men reported at least one persistent symptom complex, with women report-ing a 4point higher Post-COVID Syndrome Score on the 0-59 scale. Results from stepwise linear regression models confirm statistically significant sex differences in symptom burden that mostly withstood adjustment for medical composition and social stressors. Accounting for perceived stress and resilience attenuated them by roughly one third, leaving a substantial and statistically significant residual gap between women and men. Overall, these findings suggest that sex differences in post-COVID-19 symptoms are bound up with differences in stress exposure and coping resources, and, thus, complement biological explanations.

articles.title: Algorithmic Patriarchy: Artificial Intelligence, the Feminisation of Poverty, and the Limits of Governance
articles.abstract: Nearly fifty years after Diana Pearce named the feminisation of poverty, the systems now deciding who gets hired, credited, or cared for were trained on the same discourse that has kept it in place. Patriarchal capitalist structures have long depended on women's unpaid labour while excluding women from the rewards of the economy they sustain. Neoliberal governance extended that arrangement, swapping a structural vocabulary of poverty for one of resilience, self-improvement, and personal responsibility. The neoliberal discourse brought the shrinking of the welfare state, and with it, a new vocabulary that spread from policy papers to self-help writing, human resources content, and coaching material. It has been produced at internet scale for four decades through the same text now training large language models (LLMs). Currently, this new vocabulary is embedded in the systems that screen résumés, and intertwined with the caseworkers who draft eligibility determinations. To understand algorithmic patriarchy and its relationship with the feminisation of poverty, this paper connects two bodies of scholarship: work on how neoliberal governance produces individualising discourse, and work on how AI systems inherit bias from training data. My contribution is to name and trace the mechanism by which patriarchy, neoliberalism, and unconscious bias combine to produce a vocabulary, reproduced by artificial intelligence systems, that may sustain the feminisation of poverty. Current governance frameworks audit outcomes but not the discourse producing them. This paper argues that language matters, and that identifying the unconscious bias it carries is a precondition for its measurement and correction – the basis on which governance bodies can design policies bypassing their own invisible limitations.

articles.title: Inside the meat locker: anticipatory self-censorship and pressure on the vocabulary of American science
articles.abstract: The U.S. federal grant terminations of 2025 have had a chilling effect on American science. Grantees whose awards have been renegotiated under threat of termination must now determine how the revised terms constrain the language they use when reporting their findings in peer-reviewed publications. Standing in the meat locker of anticipatory compliance, scientists face strong incentives to adopt conservative interpretations of what the revised terms require. In this commentary, I describe a case that surfaced during editorial review, in which an author excised disfavored terminology from a manuscript. Manuscript-level effects of this kind will ordinarily be invisible because pre-submission sanitization leaves no observable counterfactual in the published record. My concerns about the implications for the field are grounded in three recent episodes in U.S. history—the freeze on federal funding for gun violence research; the near-elimination and ongoing dismantling of the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality; and the Toomey “hit list” of grants on HIV prevention and sexual behavior—each of which had durable adverse consequences for American science even without the backing of Stalinist repression. The post-Lysenko experience suggests that even if formal restrictions can be imposed and rescinded rapidly, the damage to human capital, training pipelines, and institutional trust may outlive the political conditions that produced them. Author-side strategies for lexical compliance (awkward periphrases, coded substitutions, and portfolio segregation) offer little defense against a determined state adversary. Their principal virtue is to make private accommodations visible as coordinated acts performed under duress—which is not nothing, because scientists deserve to have their compliance recorded accurately as compliance rather than as consent.

articles.title: The Fruits of Finitude: Reflexive Minimalism in Epistemology and Ethics
articles.abstract:
Reflexive Minimalism is a foundational paper proposing a minimal criterion for epistemic and normative stability: reflexive stability. A claim or norm is admissible only if it can survive its own application and does not undermine the conditions of reasoning, justification, or disagreement.

The paper begins from epistemic finitude: finite agents cannot certify possession of final, unquestionable truth about ultimate reality. This does not imply relativism. Rather, it motivates reflexive humility: truth may be sought seriously, but no finite agent may treat their grasp of it as absolute possession.

Applied to ethics, the framework rejects coercion grounded in uncertifiable ultimate claims and protects the shared space in which reasons can be given, challenged, and revised.

This text serves as the programmatic foundation for a broader research project. A shorter core statement and further focused spin-offs will develop selected implications of the framework in epistemology, ethics, and related fields.

articles.title: Double Robust, Flexible Adjustment Methods for Causal Inference: An Overview and an Evaluation
articles.abstract: Double robust methods for flexible covariate adjustment in causal inference have proliferated in recent years. Despite their apparent advantages in overcoming model misspecification, these methods are rarely used by social scientists. It is also unclear whether these methods actually outperform more traditional methods in finite samples. This paper has two aims: It is a guide to some of the latest methods in double robust, flexible covariate adjustment using machine learning, and it tests them against more traditional statistical methods and flexible, non-double robust methods using simulated, cross-sectional data where the treatment effect is known. Double robust methods covered include Augmented Inverse Probability Weighting (AIPW), Targeted Maximum Likelihood Estimation (TMLE), and Double/Debiased Machine Learning (DML). Results suggest that these methods do outperform traditional methods in a wide range of simulations, but only when paired with flexible machine learning estimators. Notably, G-computation with the same flexible estimators obtains almost identical results, and standard regression methods have only slightly higher bias. In the scenarios considered in this paper, flexibility and robustness to heterogeneous treatment effects appear to be more important properties than double robustness.

articles.title: Agent-based Modeling and Simulations
articles.abstract: Computational modeling and simulations have become increasingly relevant in the social sciences, offering powerful approaches for studying complex social phenomena. This chapter focuses on agent-based modeling (ABM) and its advantages for computational communication researchers, particularly for those who are just starting out. We introduce ABM, explain its core principles, and explore different types of models and their purposes. Through illustrative examples, we show how ABM has been and can be applied to address important research questions in communication science and related disciplines. The chapter then provides a practical step-by-step guide for conducting simulation research, outlining each step of the modeling cycle according to established methodological standards. We also highlight the importance of transparency and reproducibility through open science practices. Finally, we discuss emerging trends, such as the integration of large language models, which may shape the future of computational modeling and simulations in our field. This chapter aims to equip researchers, especially beginners in computational communication science, with a solid conceptual foundation and practical tools for incorporating ABM into their work.

articles.title: Canvassing Mobilizes and Increases Vote Share: Evidence from a Local Election in Seattle
articles.abstract: A long line of research has shown that door-to-door canvassing is a potent campaign tactic for increasing turnout and, in some cases, vote share. More recent work has theorized, however, that canvassing effects are largest in low-salience elections without party cues and concentrated among occasional voters canvassed closer to Election Day. In this research note, I test these theoretical expectations by examining the effect of canvassing in a February local election in Seattle for a housing-related ballot measure. Using a novel geo-coded dataset of seventy doorknocking campaigns over three months, I find that voters more proximate to canvassing operations were more likely to vote and that proximate precincts had a slightly higher vote share for the targeted ballot measure. Moreover, consistent with recent theorizing, I find that turnout effects were concentrated among targeted Democrats canvassed soon before the election.

articles.title: The sociolinguistic labor of incarcerated people
articles.authors: Gabriella Licata; Robert Tyler; Mesro Coles; Anthony Habib Watkins; Brian Asey Gonsoulin
articles.abstract: Through participatory action research, we draw on interviews with 40 incarcerated students to examine how linguistic practices are shaped by institutional power in carceral environments. We argue that the magnitude of surveillance under incarceration produces sociolinguistic labor: the effortful management of one’s communicative repertoire. Our analysis identifies a distinctive form of dual-direction sociolinguistic labor, whereby incarcerated individuals are required to extend their repertoires both toward stigmatized vernaculars to gain social capital and toward hyperstandardized registers for institutional capital. We examine this dynamic across educational, social, and procedural domains, with particular attention to boardspeak—an emotionally-constrained, bureaucratic register through which rehabilitation is performed and assessed at a Board of Parole hearing. By situating these practices within broader critical linguistic theories and perspectives, we show incarcerated people self-surveil and create, prompting varying levels of sociolinguistic labor and innovation that are mediated by race, ethnicity, ability, socioeconomic class, and in-group membership. These findings demonstrate how high-stakes, surveilled environments intensify the stakes of language use and reshape the boundaries of communicative agency.

articles.title: Sufism, Politics and Violence: Reading Notes
articles.abstract: This paper attempts to shed some light on the nexus “Sufism-Politics-Violence” and to show how Sufism, like other religious currents, spans a wide spectrum and how it would be misleading to consider Sufis’ approach to politics and violence in an indiscriminate way. The aim is to draw the attention of academics and policy makers to the fact that opposing Sufis to other Islamic currents such as the Muslim Brotherhood, the Salafis or the Tablighis is not the right way to prevent or counter extremism. On the contrary, such an approach is not only ineffective but may be counterproductive and prompt sectarian violence.

articles.title: Addressing Violence and Extremism: The Importance of Terminology
articles.abstract: The aim of this paper is to provide some elements that will hopefully contribute to a more accurate definition of the terms used in the context of extremism and violence, to attempt a descriptive model of the extremization process that encompasses the various paths leading to violence, and to discuss the various approaches to de-extremization. Contrary to the claim of some proponents of hard security approaches, explaining extremism and terrorism is not equivalent to justifying such phenomena. Understanding the process of extremization is a necessity for all those responsible for peace and security because it enables them to deal with it more effectively. Since “violent extremism” is often used to refer to Islamic contexts, which is in itself problematic, there will be some focus on the Islamic perspective in this paper.

articles.title: Four Criteria for Differentiating Religious Entities
articles.abstract: The attitude towards religion and an undifferentiated approach of religious currents result in many contexts in disastrous policies that cause undesired tensions in both Muslim and non-Muslim societies. This paper presents four criteria that help approaching religious currents in a differentiated way, considering their non-homogeneity and the wide diversity within them.

articles.title: Uncovering the Hidden Magnitude of Within-Race/Ethnicity Skin Tone Inequality
articles.authors: Luyin Zhang; Varsha Menon; Sam Trejo
articles.abstract: Decades of research have linked skin tone to meaningful inequalities in health and social outcomes among individuals in the same self-identified racial/ethnic group. Yet efforts to document and understand within-race/ethnicity skin tone stratification have been hampered by a fundamental data problem: in most social surveys and biomedical databases, skin tone is either not collected or measured imprecisely using coarse categories based on a single observer’s judgment. In this study, we begin by conducting an online survey to quantify the reliability of existing interviewer-rated skin tone measures. Then, using elastic net regression, we build a genomic prediction model for skin tone among Black and Hispanic participants in the Add Health study, with the goal of improving the accuracy and availability of skin tone measurement in admixed populations. Finally, we use these DNA-based skin tone measures in two longitudinal studies to explore within-race/ethnicity skin tone inequality in contemporary America. Predicted skin tone yields substantially steeper gradients in socioeconomic status and racial classification, indicating that interviewer-rated measures meaningfully understate the degree of social stratification operating within racialized groups. Our results suggest that genetically derived skin tone predictions represent a promising new tool for advancing research on colorism – and, via the ancestry disequilibrium regression framework we introduce, a path toward identifying the causal effects of skin tone.

articles.title: The Role of Advisers in Mediating Worldview Conflicts
articles.abstract: Mediation as an assisted negotiation is a complex process involving the parties in conflict and a third party (the mediator/facilitator), as well as several “fourth parties” who can either be “constructive contributors” with a beneficial role, who help support and steer the process in a positive direction, promote understanding, and encourage open communication to help the parties reach a resolution, or “spoilers” with a harmful role, who obstruct, disrupt, or undermine the process, often creating conflict or preventing resolution. A good mediation process design is one that identifies from the outset all constructive contributors and harnesses their beneficial role, as well as all spoilers and neutralizes their potential harm. This contribution addresses the role of advisers in mediation processes and presents examples of the involvement of advisers in processes conducted by Cordoba Peace Institute – Geneva (CPI) over the last two decades in relation to worldview conflicts.

articles.title: Waiting Spaces as Mental Health 'Gyms': A Research through Design Framework for the Situated Activation of Wellbeing Micropractices Where People, Time, and Infrastructure Converge
articles.abstract:
Cities have expanded access to physical wellbeing by placing exercise equipment in parks and public squares: infrastructure can offer opportunities for practice without requiring a gym, a fee, or deliberate search. This study asks whether a similar logic can extend to everyday mental wellbeing: can urban infrastructure facilitate voluntary activation of wellbeing micropractices where people, time, and urban infrastructure already converge, without additional time, financial cost, or specialized access?
Using a Research through Design (RtD) approach, this study develops the Wellbeing Practices in Waiting Spaces (WPWS) framework through four phases: (1) qualitative clinical exploration using Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis (N = 8); (2) iterative design and urban prototyping in Amsterdam, Milan, and Barcelona; (3) exploration of everyday appropriation across seven countries (N = 41); and (4) comparative analysis of public-space wellbeing interventions. Low rates of voluntary flow interruption in high-flow contexts were treated as a generative finding, suggesting that instrumental movement may constrain attentional availability, leading the inquiry toward stationary contexts: waiting spaces.
Three interdependent components of situated activation emerged: (1) spatio-temporal conditions shaping attentional availability (when); (2) inner human capacities, including mindfulness, appreciation, and compassion (what); and (3) visual mediating devices providing legible, brief, voluntary invitations to wellbeing micropractices (how). Across the urban prototypes, voluntary flow interruption, defined as stopping for ≥5 seconds, ranged from 1% to 5%. In Phase 3, 85.4% of participants reported mentally repeating the phrase, and 60.9% reported sharing it.
WPWS is proposed as a transferable design architecture rather than a fixed intervention. It reconceptualizes waiting spaces as an underused spatio-temporal condition for situated activation, while recognizing that this proposition has not yet been empirically tested against other urban contexts. The findings do not establish causal or clinical effects, but provide a foundation for investigating how existing urban infrastructure can expand everyday access to wellbeing practices.
Keywords: Urban wellbeing; Waiting spaces; Latent wellbeing infrastructure; Situated activation; Mental health equity; Trauma-informed design; Wellbeing micropractices.

articles.title: The Paperwork of Grief: Administrative Burden as a Defence Against Death Exposure in Clinical Care
articles.abstract: Administrative work (documentation, the electronic record, the proliferation of meetings, the referral of distress onward to specialists) is treated almost universally in the clinician-wellbeing literature as a cause of burnout to be measured and reduced. This paper argues that in the most death-saturated settings of medicine (the cancer ward, the intensive care unit, the palliative service) that same burden may also do something the literature has not noticed: function as a social defence against sustained exposure to dying, offering clinicians a bounded, completable, finite task to retreat into when the bedside offers only problems that often end in death. The argument revives Isabel Menzies Lyth’s 1959 account of hospital routine as a collective defence against anxiety and brings it forward to the era of the electronic record, joining four literatures (on documentation burden, on death exposure and numbing, on terror management, and on the social defences of institutions) that have not previously been read together. If the conjecture holds, the prevailing prescription to strip administration away on efficiency grounds alone risks removing an unrecognised container without supplying a deliberate one, and the proper task is not to reduce paperwork but to distinguish what merely numbs from what genuinely contains, and to design containment for those who work among the dead. The claim is interpretive and bounded to high-mortality settings; the paper sets out how it could be tested and the competing explanations it complements rather than displaces.

articles.title: The Social Stratification in Generative Artificial Intelligence Literacy, Use Frequency, and Workplace Acceptance in 11 European countries
articles.authors: zhuofei lu; Yao Ma; Wei Zhuang; Yucheng He
articles.abstract:
Generative AI (GenAI) has diffused rapidly across Europe, yet who feels able to
use it—and who is willing to work with it—remains poorly understood. Using the
latest CRONOS-3 panel of the probability-based European Social Survey (N =
7,556; 11 European countries, fielded in 2025), we model six separate measures
of GenAI literacy and use frequency, together with acceptance of GenAI as an
assistant and as a peer in the workplace, using country-clustered estimators with
wild-bootstrap inference. Acceptance is strongly role-differentiated: a majority
accept GenAI as an assistant, but only one in ten as a peer. Both competence and
acceptance are sharply stratified by education, age, and gender—and the gender
divide is the most consistent pattern of all: women trail men on every one of the
six literacy and use measures and on both acceptance outcomes, and the deficit
appears in behavioural use as well as in self-assessed skill, so it cannot be reduced
to gendered self-assessment alone. GenAI literacy and use frequency in turn
strongly predict acceptance in both roles. Cross-national variation is substantial,
but with only 11 countries no association between national media, scholarly, or
AI-talent environments and individual outcomes survives strict small-cluster and
multiple-testing corrections, so national context is treated descriptively. GenAI
competence and workplace acceptance thus emerge as socially stratified from the
outset—with women consistently furthest behind—an early-forming divide that
risks hardening as GenAI becomes workplace infrastructure.

articles.title: The Selective Politicization of Diversity Advertising
articles.authors: A.I. Loureiro Lopes; Alberto Lopez Ortega; Mariken Anna Catharina Geertruida van der Velden
articles.abstract: Corporations increasingly feature minority families in mainstream advertising, positioning themselves as inclusive civic actors. Yet whether audiences read such representation as ordinary marketing or as a political statement—and whether all minorities are read alike—remains unclear. We field a pre-registered survey experiment in the Netherlands (N≈1,500), randomly exposing respondents to a supermarket advertisement depicting a control (white, heterosexual), Muslim, or same-sex family. Minority-family advertisements are perceived as substantially more political than the control and shift perceptions of the brand to the ideological left, both in abstract placement and in concrete party association. These effects are markedly selective: the Muslim-family advertisement is read as roughly twice as political as the same-sex advertisement, and is the only condition to lower purchase intention, and does so precisely through the perception that it is political. Issue attributions are domain-specific: the same-sex advertisement moves perceived brand support for LGBTQ+ rights, the Muslim advertisement perceived support for immigration—and, contrary to expectations, these reactions are broad rather than confined to right-wing consumers. The findings reveal a selective politicization of corporate inclusion, in which ethno-religious diversity is politicized and commercially penalized while sexual-orientation diversity is comparatively normalized.

articles.title: When Does Generative AI Become a Developmental Resource? A Multilevel Taxonomy of Enactment Conditions
articles.authors: Andreea Nicolau; Sonja Rispens; Pascale Marie Le Blanc; Kees Maton; Piet J. R. van Gool; Ad Kleingeld
articles.abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) creates a developmental ambiguity for organizations: it can support learning, reflection, and judgment, but it can also accelerate task completion while reducing engagement with the cognitive and social processes through which capabilities develop. This study asks which multilevel conditions shape whether GenAI is enacted as a resource for learning and continuous development or as a shortcut for task completion. Drawing on an inductive, multi-stakeholder qualitative study with 41 organizational actors, we use thematic analysis to identify empirical categories and morphological principles to organize them into a multidimensional taxonomy of GenAI enactment. The taxonomy identifies four interrelated dimensions: Organizational Conditions, Capability Conditions, Decision Drivers, and GenAI Enactment. Interpreting these findings through the automation–augmentation paradox, we show that automation- and augmentation-oriented uses are not fixed properties of technologies or tasks but contextually produced orientations shaped by an iterative system of societal/institutional, organizational, and individual-related conditions. The study contributes to AI and management research by specifying the condition architecture through which GenAI becomes more or less developmental in practice. We argue that learning-oriented GenAI integration requires attention to the multilevel conditions that preserve verification, reflection, feedback, and accountable judgment when task completion no longer necessarily develops capability.

articles.title: Climate policy is domestic politics: Mechanisms shaping the political feasibility of mitigation
articles.authors: E. Keith Smith; Christina Eder; Sarah Gomm; Gabriele Spilker; Isabelle Stadelmann-Steffen
articles.abstract: The Paris Agreement shifted the central challenge of climate mitigation from international burden-sharing to domestic politics. In high-emitting countries, the binding constraint on near-term emissions cuts is no longer the absence of effective policy instruments, but their political feasibility, that is, governments' capacity and willingness to adopt, implement, and sustain mitigation policy over time. We review the political feasibility of climate mitigation along four dimensions: stakeholder interests and influence, public opinion and social norms, political-economic context and institutional constraints, and distributional effects and inequality. Using the policymaking process as our analytical lens, we trace how these dimensions hinder or enable mitigation at successive stages of agenda-setting, formulation, and implementation. We synthesise this literature into a practical framework for making mitigation politically feasible, identify a set of persistent misconceptions that obstruct progress, and outline near-term actions that the evidence supports. The central challenge of mitigation is no longer identifying effective instruments, but making them politically feasible under real-world conditions.

articles.title: Corruption in Nepal's Local Governments: A Case Study of Institutional Weaknesses and Citizen Outcomes
articles.abstract: This case study deals with corruption in public procurement at the local government level in Nepal. Nepal established 753 local governments with substantial responsibility for public spending, including procurement of goods, works and services, following the adoption of the Constitution in 2015. Mostly today, public spending is the responsibility of local governments, especially on capital investment in infrastructure, such as roads, schools, health facilities and water supply systems. But the speed of devolution of responsibilities has not been matched by adequate systems of transparency, accountability and integrity. This paper explores the nature and extent of corruption in local government procurement in Nepal, drawing on publicly available data from the Commission for the Investigation of Abuse of Authority, Transparency International, the World Bank, the Asian Development Bank and government audit reports. The analysis shows that procurement is a high-risk area for corruption at the local level. Corrupt practices are many and include bid-rigging, inflated costs, shoddy work, kickbacks, collusion among bidders, political interference with contract awards, etc. The data show that many local governments do not follow procurement rules well, publish limited information and have weak oversight. Audit reports frequently find irregularities in procurement by local government. The paper investigates factors leading to procurement corruption including weak institutional capacity, political interference, lack of transparency, limited oversight by citizens and poor enforcement. The report ends with recommendations for improving procurement integrity, including better procurement rules, more transparency, capacity building, stronger oversight, more citizen participation, and accountability enforcement.

articles_hidden.title: Elite-Public Gaps on Salient Foreign Policy Issues: Experimental Evidence from the 2022/23 US Sanctions on Russia
articles_hidden.authors: Anton Peez; Felix Bethke; Felix S. Bethke
articles_hidden.abstract: Do citizens and political elites in Western democracies hold different views on foreign policy? ‘Elite-public gaps’ raise questions about whether elites represent public preferences and how much discretion they exercise. Research suggests that although gaps exist, they are significantly driven by ‘mundane’ compositional differences. We examine these gaps during the 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine. We ran a paired experiment with US executive staffers (n = 253) and the US public (n = 1,002), asking whether respondents support increasing sanctions on Russia.
