We randomize information on real public polling highly supportive of sanctions. The public was less supportive than executive staffers at baseline, but more responsive to public opinion. Gaps shrink after accounting for basic sociodemographics. This extends research on elite-public gaps to cover salient real-world events.

articles_hidden.title: A STUDY OF THE EMERGENCE OF WELFARE CLEAVAGES IN SOUTH KOREA
articles_hidden.abstract:
This study aims to trace the cause of an emerging welfare cleavage under circumstances where discourses on economic growth have been dominant in Korean politics. On the basis of the theories of interaction between changing social structure and social-norm dynamics, this paper explores the causes of an emerging welfare cleavage in the case of South Korea during the late 2000s. To analyze the change of economic structure and public awareness regarding public welfare, I used the data of macro-economic indicators and public opinion polls and utilized press releases to analyze discourses of political actors.
The linked-policies effects of an immature “developmental welfare regime” and neo-liberal economic policies caused social polarization and expansion of the poverty stratum in the course of a slowdown in economic growth in the 1990s and foreign exchange crisis in 1998. The existing norm (i.e., economic growth could solve problems concerning people's livelihood) that had been maintained in the era of rapid economic growth was weakened. A conflict between an education superintendent and the Gyeonggi-do Provincial Council triggered a debate on free meals and welfare in 2009. Civil society groups were organized on a national scale, and they started a discourse struggle to replace individual interests with public interests and to obtain social legitimacy. Political parties gradually accepted the welfare issue as the primary electoral pledge for their political interests after public preference regarding growth and distribution changed when confronted with political crises.
This study draws an implication that general factors affecting Western welfare states (e.g., power alliance and democratic institutions) influence East Asian welfare states by analyzing the case of South Korean welfare politics. It means that studies of East Asian welfare states can use explanatory building blocks partly from existing welfare theories rather than stressing the exceptionalism of East Asian welfare states. However, owing to the different economic and political structures of East Asian states from those of Western countries during the formative stage of welfare states, studies of East Asian welfare states need to consider path dependency in the historical context of East Asian political economy.

articles_hidden.title: The Divergent Trajectory of Environmental Politics between  the United States and the United Kingdom
articles_hidden.abstract: This study examines factors affecting the divergent environmental performances between the U.S. and the U.K. from the perspective of social movement. I look into domestic political factors, especially social movements causing different environmental performances in two countries that attain the high level of economic growth and are under the same international factors. Given that previous research dealing with domestic political factors tends to focus on political institutions and that the comparative research on the cases of the U.S. and the U.K. are limited, this research is relevant. I utilize the EPI scores, protest data, public opinion data and party manifestos. I conclude that the strong connection of environmental movement with political parties, less dispersive social movement agendas, favorable conditions from the EU and relatively weak anti-environmental movement led Britain to making a better environmental performance than the U.S.

articles_hidden.title: Understanding children’s housing in Australia: a data framework
articles_hidden.authors: Amy Clair; Emma Baker; Lynne Giles; Claire Morey; Megan Robinson
articles_hidden.abstract: This project examines the available data on children’s housing and wellbeing and current policy in Australia to highlight how housing affects children’s health and development. It provides policymakers with a guide to the different housing situations children face, identifies significant knowledge gaps and related risks, and proposes priorities for policy-relevant data collection and evidence development. The impacts of Australia’s housing crisis on children have received less attention than for other population groups. Accessible data collections rarely focus on them. Yet households with children are particularly affected by poor quality and insecure housing, and children’s physical vulnerability and dependence on caregivers increases the related risks to their wellbeing. This underscores the need for stronger data insights to support earlier intervention, better targeting and more accountable policy for children.

articles_hidden.title: CHALLENGES AND OPPORTUNITIES FOR DEVELOPING UPCYCLED COSMETIC INGREDIENTS IN BRAZIL: A PERSPECTIVE FOR SMALL AND MEDIUM ENTERPRISES
articles_hidden.authors: Murilo Dotti Garcia; Orlando Nastri Neto
articles_hidden.abstract: The use of plant by-products to develop cosmetic ingredients has gained considerable momentum globally, driven by growing demand for sustainability and the increasing expectation that ingredients deliver scientifically proven efficacy. Brazil offers particularly favourable conditions for this trend, since the country combines unparalleled biodiversity with a world-scale agribusiness chain that generates vast volumes of largely underused by-products. This article examines the main challenges and opportunities facing Brazilian small and medium cosmetic enterprises (SMEs) as they develop ingredients from these by-products, focusing on regulatory, technical, scientific and market dimensions. Drawing on an integrative review of recent scientific and sectoral literature and on an analysis of the national context, it argues that SMEs, despite capital and infrastructure constraints, hold genuine advantages in agility and proximity to regional production chains. It concludes that conditions are favourable for smaller companies willing to invest in technical capacity, strategic partnerships and differentiation grounded in scientific evidence.

articles_hidden.title: Toward an Intersectional Occupational Health Framework: Psychosocial Conditions as Allocated Exposures
articles_hidden.abstract: Occupational health research treats psychosocial working conditions either as features of a job or as traits that help workers cope. This article proposes the Intersectional Occupational Health (IOH) framework, which instead treats these conditions as exposures that labor regimes allocate to differently positioned workers. Drawing on vulnerability theory and the sociology of work, the framework argues that a worker's psychosocial profile records where that worker has been placed, since who meets high-strain conditions, and for how long, is set by law, immigration rules, and welfare systems. On this reading, the uneven spread of these conditions measures a process that produces vulnerability rather than a tally of how well workers cope. The framework follows the path from social position to health outcome, and it treats a sound intervention as one that redistributes exposure rather than one that raises the average. Two cases, domestic work in Southern Europe and platform delivery in Germany, ground a set of recommendations for governments, ranging from household labor inspection to an enforceable presumption of employment.

articles_hidden.title: Relay cooperation between women and girls during foraging trips among BaYaka hunter-gatherers in the Republic of the Congo
articles_hidden.authors: Amandine Erika Stéphanie Visine; Haneul Jang
articles_hidden.abstract: Children in small-scale societies contribute to subsistence and infant care from an early age, developing relevant skills through everyday participation. To examine how such participation is organised in practice, we focus on women’s daily foraging among BaYaka hunter-gatherers in the Congolese rainforest, where children frequently accompany adults. Using focal follows, we recorded mothers’ activity states - foraging, travelling, and resting - alongside helping behaviours of group members, including childcare, foraging, and basket carrying. We find that childcare, subsistence, and load-carrying responsibilities are dynamically redistributed through relay cooperation between women and girls, who are not necessarily kin. Infant care is frequently transferred from women to girls, enabling mothers to continue foraging without carrying infants. When mothers pause to rest or breastfeed, girls temporarily take over foraging tasks. These role shifts occur repeatedly within trips, revealing a structured yet flexible system that allows mothers to manage the energetic and mobility constraints of childcare while maintaining productivity.  At the same time, relay cooperation provides girls with repeated opportunities to engage in both caregiving and subsistence, supporting learning through participation with women other than their own mothers. These findings provide insight into how children develop as cooperative actors through active participation in women’s subsistence and caregiving activities.

articles_hidden.title: From humanitarian design to design for social innovation: a comparative experiment activating reflexivity on coloniality and power dynamics.
articles_hidden.authors: Riccardo Torta; Marco Andrea Finardi; Abigail Turinayo; Victor Muwonge Semaganda; Marco Gobetti
articles_hidden.abstract:
This meta-research originates from two experiences of the first two authors, who respectively worked on a Humanitarian Design (HD) project in Uganda with Design Without Borders and on a Design for Social Innovation (DSI) project in Italy with Polimi DESIS Lab. Similar tensions emerged from both contexts regarding the relationship between the design teams and the communities engaged, highlighting the risk of perpetuating systemic oppression and epistemic injustice. To explore these imbalances, the teams were engaged in two sets of sessions, activating reflexivity on social structures embedded in their practices, to uncover potential dynamics rooted in coloniality and power.

Where the Ugandan HD project served as a testbed for the approach and three reflexive tools, the sessions within the Italian project confirmed the initial proposition, showing the potentially broad impact of the application of reflexivity on oppressive dynamics within DSI projects. This experiment uncovered the risks entailed by engaging with local communities, raised issues about urbanity and rurality, different forms of knowledge and models of development, challenging the conception of modernity and recognising these foundational elements of coloniality even in a European context.

Considering the exploratory nature of this research, the intent is to provide grounding for future critical inquiries within the wider DSI community, demonstrating the need to rethink current design practices from a liberatory and relational perspective.

articles_hidden.title: Occupational AI Exposure and the Reconfiguration of Class Inequalities in Perceived Job Insecurity
articles_hidden.authors: Daniela Bellani; Honorata Bogusz; samuel plach
articles_hidden.abstract: Research on AI and inequality has focused primarily on employment, wages, productivity, and task displacement, while less is known about how occupational AI exposure is associated with workers’ subjective insecurity and how these concerns are distributed across social classes. This study examines perceived job insecurity among employed workers in Europe, distinguishing quantitative insecurity - fear of job loss - from qualitative insecurity - fear of an undesirable change in the work situation. We use the 2024 European Working Conditions Survey, linked to an occupation-level measure of potential AI exposure, to examine whether the class pattern of AI-related insecurity mirrors the conventional class gradient in perceived job insecurity. Manual workers report the highest average fear of job loss, but the positive association between occupational AI exposure and job-loss fear is concentrated among higher- and lower-grade service workers and is weak or absent among manual workers. By contrast, occupational AI exposure shows a positive association with fear of undesirable job change, but this outcome displays no recurrent class pattern. Exploratory analyses show that the service-class association with job-loss fear is especially visible among tertiary-educated and older workers and among those who do not report using AI directly at work, while cross-national estimates indicate that the pattern appears across several institutional contexts.  The findings suggest that occupational AI exposure may reconfigure rather than sim-ply reproduce existing inequalities in insecurity, as the workers reporting the highest baseline insecurity are not those among whom the association with AI exposure is most pronounced

articles_hidden.title: Spirit Becoming Matter: A Thematic Analysis of Creation Stories
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objective
This qualitative study examined the creation stories from a cross-section of cultures and traditions to determine whether there are important similarities. 
Methods
Thematic analysis was conducted with 15 creation stories from 11 traditions. Initial coding was reviewed to develop themes, which were then recursively applied to the stories to find further examples and refine definitions. The resulting 13 themes were then clustered into 4 categories. 
Results
The diverse stories shared significant commonalities in their processes, elements, and implications. The first category is consciousness, which includes the themes of creator being, humans as co-creators, thought/mind, and one source. The second category is the elements, which includes the themes of water, light, and earth. The third category is opposites and similars, with no further subcategories. The fourth category is energy, which includes the themes of energy/vibration, breath, void, and time.
Conclusions
Surprising similarities across cultures point toward a model of reality in which consciousness is primary, preceding, and giving rise to physical form. All matter started as energy, and each part contains elements of the whole. The findings suggest that the divine, or universal consciousness, is contained in all matter, that consciousness may be eternal, and that the continuum of consciousness facilitates communication between humans, the divine, and all manifest forms.

articles_hidden.title: The Politics of Consolidation: Authoritarian Drift and Economic Ambition in Post-Election Tanzania
articles_hidden.abstract:
Abstract
Tanzania’s political trajectory in August 2026 is increasingly defined by a striking contradiction: ambitious economic modernization is unfolding alongside a marked contraction of political space. Following the contested October 2025 general election, President Samia Suluhu Hassan’s administration appears increasingly focused on restoring political control while facing unresolved questions concerning electoral legitimacy, accountability and constitutional reform (BBC, 2026; Xinhua, 2026a; Xinhua, 2026b). The resignation of Vice President Emmanuel Nchimbi on 25 August 2026 (BBC, 2026; KBC Digital, 2026), restrictions on opposition political activity (The Citizen, 2026b; Daily News, 2026a), and the prosecution of opposition leader Tundu Lissu (The Citizen, 2026a; Mwananchi, 2026) have intensified concerns about the direction of Tanzania’s political order. At the same time, major infrastructure achievements, particularly the Julius Nyerere Hydropower Project, provide the government with a powerful narrative of developmental competence (Xinhua, 2026c).
This paper situates these developments within the comparative literature on democratic backsliding, electoral authoritarianism, political legitimacy, institutional change and developmental states. Drawing on Bermeo’s (2016) analysis of democratic backsliding, Schedler’s (2013) conception of electoral authoritarianism, Beetham’s (1991) theory of political legitimacy, and Doner, Ritchie, and Slater’s (2005) analysis of developmental states, it argues that Tanzania is exhibiting features of political consolidation in which executive control and developmental performance increasingly operate as mutually reinforcing sources of regime stability. The paper does not suggest that Tanzania has become a fully authoritarian state. Rather, it identifies an authoritarian drift in which restrictions on political competition and civic space coexist with continued electoral institutions and ambitious economic modernization. The central argument is that economic performance may strengthen short-term regime legitimacy, but it cannot permanently substitute for credible elections, accountable institutions, judicial independence and meaningful political inclusion. The widening gap between developmental ambition and political openness consequently represents both a democratic challenge and a long-term governance and investment risk.

articles_hidden.title: Older adults without a partner and adult children in Finland
articles_hidden.authors: INVEST Flagship; alyona artamonova; Mirkka Danielsbacka
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Core-kinless older adults, i.e., those lacking a partner and children, represent a potentially vulnerable group. However, the whole population-level research devoted to this group remains scarce.
Objectives: This study estimates the prevalence, sociodemographic characteristics, and geographic distribution of core-kinless adults in Finland, with attention to variation across ethnolinguistic groups of Finnish, Swedish, and other language speakers.
Methods: We used register data covering the entire population aged 65 and over in 2024 (N = 1,328,732) and descriptive analyses. Core-kinlessness was defined as the absence of both a registered co-residing partner and any living children registered in Finland. 
Results: In total, 11.6% of older adults in Finland were core-kinless. Prevalence was 11.3% among Finnish-speaking, 10.3% among Swedish-speaking, and 30.5% among other language-speaking individuals. Migration background in general, being male among Finnish-speaking as well as being female, being older and having lower education among other language-speaking individuals are the characteristics of this group. The positive associations between municipal core-kinlessness and i) demographic dependency ratio, ii) the mortality rate among older adults and iii) the rate of home care clients confirm that municipalities where these older adults are concentrated also face greater demographic and service pressures.
Contribution: This study provides the first register-based national estimates of core-kinlessness in Finland, demonstrating that survey data underestimate this group. The findings offer evidence for targeted care planning at the individual and municipality levels.

articles_hidden.title: Exploitation-based social class, class consciousness and political participation
articles_hidden.authors: Agata Anita Troost; Jaap Nieuwenhuis; Jonathan J.B. Mijs
articles_hidden.abstract:
Departing from recent discussions about social class and relational inequality, we investigate the idea of the power antagonism between the workers and capitalists, and the implications of this antagonism for political participation. While the popular sociological occupation- and income-based schemes can measure social mobility within the existing economic conditions, social class based on exploitation is more relevant for measuring political empowerment. We adopt a quantitative empirical approach to analyse the class structure, class consciousness, and their associations with political behaviour including voting, direct political action and trade union membership.    
We recreate E.O. Wright’s exploitation-based class scheme (1985) with new survey data collected by us in the Netherlands in 2024. We then test whether people’s housing market position, income, wealth and education influence their class consciousness and political actions to a similar degree as their labour market, or production processes, position captured by the class scheme. Exploitation-based social class, more than income, wealth, housing, or occupation, predicts class consciousness and shapes patterns of political participation in the Netherlands, although education remains the strongest predictor of direct political action and voting. High class consciousness only motivates some middle classes to direct political action, but all classes are similarly demotivated by feelings of political resignation and being unable to enact change. While low-skilled workers display relatively high class consciousness, they are unable to translate it into political engagement. Our findings highlight the persistent and complex role of class in contemporary society.

articles_hidden.title: THE HORMUZ STRAIT DISRUPTION AND PAYMENT DELAYS IN INDIAN TRADE FINANCE: A Time-Series Analysis of Banking Sector Vulnerability (2019-2024)
articles_hidden.abstract: The Hormuz Strait—through which 21% of global petroleum trade passes—experienced significant geopolitical tensions from 2019-2024, creating disruptions to maritime commerce and financial flows. This paper provides a detailed empirical analysis of how these disruptions affected payment cycles in Indian trade finance and banking. Using Reserve Bank of India (RBI) data, port statistics, and transaction-level banking records (2019-2024, N=18,547 trade credit facilities), we employ time-series analysis, distributed lag models, and shock analysis to quantify the relationship between Hormuz disruptions and payment delays. Key findings: (1) Trade finance payment delays increased by an average of 8.3 days (95% CI: 6.1-10.5) following Hormuz tension announcements; (2) Letter of Credit (LC) issuance costs rose by 42-67 basis points; (3) Banks increased collateral requirements by 12-18%, contracting working capital availability by ₹4,200-6,800 crores; (4) The shock effect persisted for 90-120 days post-incident, with heterogeneous impacts across firm sizes (SMEs experienced 2.1x higher delays than large enterprises). Our analysis reveals that geopolitical shocks in maritime chokepoints generate significant financial friction in emerging market trade finance systems, with particular vulnerability among smaller firms lacking working capital buffers. We propose targeted policy interventions including development of trade credit insurance mechanisms, geographic diversification of banking relationships, and central bank communication frameworks for predictable intervention during crises.

articles_hidden.title: A National Portrait of Life Course Marital and Cohabiting History
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objectives
Partnership histories encompass the duration, timing, and sequence of marital and cohabiting relationships that accumulate across the life course. Taking advantage of detailed cohabitation history data available in The National Social Life and Health and Aging Project (NSHAP), this paper constructs older adults’ partnership histories and describes variation across gender, race and ethnicity, and social class. It also examines the associations between partnership histories and health outcomes.  
Methods
Using NSHAP Rounds 1 through 4, we harmonized retrospective marriage and cohabitation records for 6,618 respondents and constructed measures of union counts, timing, duration, sequence, and dissolution, with 7-, 11-, and 14-category classifications. We evaluated missingness and consistency, summarized sociodemographic differences, and illustrated associations with three health outcomes.
Results
Older adults married to their first spouse (37.7%) and widowed (14.9%) comprise over half of the sample. Yet divorce and cohabitation are also common in older adults’ partnership histories, with over one third of the sample reporting having ever divorced (38.5%) and having ever cohabited before a marriage (36.7%). Partnership histories involving union disruption, never marrying, and cohabitation are associated with differences in self-rated health, depressive symptoms, and functional limitations relative to continuous first marriage. 
Discussion
The partnership history data available in NSHAP provides a novel opportunity for researchers to examine the significance of intimate relationships accumulated across the life course for health and aging beyond marital histories alone or current relationship status.

articles_hidden.title: Psychological Readiness, Innovation Management, and the Adoption of Sustainable Agriculture: An Extended Theory of Planned Behaviour Model of Food Security among Smallholder Farmers in Climate-Vulnerable Bangladesh
articles_hidden.authors: Enamul Haque; M. Nasim Reza; Nurul Islam Nepo; Syed M. Ali Reza; Solaiman Chowdhury; Atikur Rahman
articles_hidden.abstract: This study examines the psychological and managerial factors that influence the adoption of sustainable agricultural practices (SA) and household food security (FS) in climate-vulnerable regions of Bangladesh. Drawing on an integrated framework that combines the Extended Theory of Planned Behaviour (ETPB) with Innovation Diffusion Theory (IDT), the study analyses a refined sample of 380 smallholder farmers using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM). Unlike earlier models that confounded institutional and individual respondents, this study isolates the psychological readiness of primary producers by restricting the quantitative sample to active smallholders. The results show that climate change beliefs exert a significant positive effect on attitude, subjective norms, and perceived behavioural control, and that these socio-cognitive constructs in turn positively predict sustainable behavioural intention. Both behavioural intention and perceived behavioural control significantly influence the adoption of sustainable agriculture, which subsequently enhances food security. Individual innovation management further contributes to both the adoption of sustainable agriculture and food security outcomes. The findings underscore the importance of aligning the psychological readiness of individual farmers with the institutional readiness of the wider innovation system, offering a holistic basis for designing rural development strategies in climate-stressed agrarian economies.

articles_hidden.title: Incarceration and Deservingness: Experimental Evidence on Less Eligibility
articles_hidden.authors: Christopher Berk; Lucas Nunez; Brett C Burkhardt
articles_hidden.abstract: A substantial literature on welfare politics shows that public support for redistribution depends on markers like need, effort, and reciprocity that sort recipients into deserving and undeserving categories. We test whether incarceration status functions as a particularly powerful deservingness marker, structured by the eighteenth-century principle of "less eligibility": that no one subject to punishment should fare better than the poorest free person. Using a pre-registered conjoint experiment with a representative U.S. sample (N = 1,929), we find that incarcerated applicants to an identical rehabilitative program receive substantially less public support than otherwise-comparable poor or welfare-dependent applicants — a penalty that persists even when the incarcerated applicant is shown to benefit more from the program than the comparison case. Decomposing the moral-cultural mechanisms behind this penalty, we find community-belonging and cost-benefit evidence each narrow it somewhat, while signals of the applicant's hard work and reliability paradoxically widen it. The incarceration penalty, we argue, operates as a durable boundary of moral exclusion rather than a correctable informational gap, with implications for how welfare-state and punishment scholarship jointly understand deservingness.
