articles_hidden.title: Leveraging LLMs to assist tourists at destinations – The opportunities and risks of deploying open-source humanoid robots
articles_hidden.authors: Yash Pandey; Spencer Kayser; Marius Portmann; Siamak Layeghy; Sara Dolnicar
articles_hidden.abstract: LLMs are transforming tourist search behaviour. Tourists currently access LLMs on phones, tablets, and laptops. Open-source humanoid robots change this: the LLM becomes embodied and physically situated at the destination. This conceptual paper develops a framework for understanding the consequences of deploying open-source humanoid robots in tourism. The framework rests on two constructs. Embodied authority transfer describes how tourists reattribute LLM output from a private planning tool to the destination's official service infrastructure when delivered by a robot hosted in a tourism setting. Capability asymmetry describes the gap between what an embodied LLM can fluently discuss and what it can accurately know or actually do. The article discusses deployment scenarios and risk, and offers a detailed research agenda.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond Blame: School Violence, Youth Despair, and the Failure of Containment in Recent Philippine Shootings
articles_hidden.abstract: Recent school-related shootings in the Philippines, especially the June 2026 attack at San Jose National High School in Tacloban and the August 2026 shooting at Ateneo de Zamboanga University, generated public pressure to locate a single cause: a teacher, a game, a security failure, a disturbed child, a family failure. This paper argues that such explanations are emotionally understandable but causally insufficient. Drawing on incident reporting, official and reported-official statements, verified WHO Global School-based Student Health Survey data, DepEd Region VIII memoranda, public-health and threat-assessment literature, and C. G. Jung's Modern Man in Search of a Soul, the paper proposes a different representation: recent Philippine school violence should be understood as a failed ecology of containment. In this frame, adolescent grievance, despair, humiliation, or rupture become dangerous when they converge with firearm access, missed warning signs, weak disclosure pathways, digital scripts or grooming environments, livestream/notoriety affordances, and institutions that are not yet able to metabolize distress before it turns into public violence. The argument does not claim that Jungian "spiritual crisis" is a forensic motive. Rather, Jung helps name the meaning-layer of youth collapse: psychic pain, futurelessness, shame, and disconnection are real in their effects even when they cannot be reduced to one external cause. The paper concludes that prevention must move beyond blame toward containment: firearm accountability, threat assessment, confidential reporting, anti-bullying systems, psychosocial support, digital-platform safeguards, and living forms of youth meaning and belonging.

articles_hidden.title: Staying Long Enough to Stop Seeing: Autoethnography, Long-Term Immersion, and Tourism Research
articles_hidden.abstract: Autoethnographic tourism research has typically been based on discrete journeys or bounded periods of fieldwork, leaving the epistemological implications of long-term residential immersion comparatively underexamined. This article argues that sustained residence produces a distinctive form of knowledge grounded not simply in prolonged observation but in the transformation of perception over time. Drawing on more than a decade of living and working across Nanjing, Hangzhou, and Wenzhou, China, it proposes a three-stage framework of estrangement, normalisation, and critical re-estrangement. Initial unfamiliarity heightens attention; repeated exposure subsequently renders once-remarkable features ordinary and increasingly invisible; disciplined analytical attention can then return the researcher to these normalised environments with a capacity to recognise recurrence, pattern, and institutional continuity. Through examples of everyday urban landscapes and the seasonal infrastructure underlying Hangzhou's elevated-highway flower displays, the article demonstrates how long-term immersion makes visible processes that shorter encounters may register only as isolated events or spectacles. Critical re-estrangement therefore offers a methodological means of converting habituation from an apparent limitation of long-term residence into an analytical resource.

articles_hidden.title: Detention as a disabling institution: Age-related health disparities in the US immigration detention system
articles_hidden.abstract: From 2008 to 2018, US Immigration and Customs Enforcement apprehended over two million noncitizens in the US interior. However, data on detained immigrants' health is limited, with a particular lack of research on older detained immigrants, despite the distinct vulnerabilities aging individuals confront within and outside carceral settings. Immigrants face diverse structural challenges as they age, and incarcerated individuals experience accelerated aging and have worse health relative to non-incarcerated individuals, due to exposure to structural disadvantage, coupled with the health harms of incarceration itself. Using data from the Immigrant Detention Survey (n=495) and the National Health Interview Survey (n=8,383), and drawing on theories of aging in carceral settings, immigrant health and aging, and immigration policies as structural determinants of health, I address two critical and unresolved questions: What is the health profile of older detained adults, relative to younger adults? How do age-related health disparities among detained immigrants compare to those of non-detained immigrants? My findings reveal age-related health disparities in detained and non-detained populations. I also find much higher rates of poor health among detained immigrants than in the non-detained population, regardless of age. Results suggest immigration detention may be considered a mass disabling institution linked to poor health across the life course and may exacerbate age-related disparities, highlighting the need for more humane and equitable immigration and health policies.
